moves.spoken: Against a strong opponent we bring out our real weapon — the Ruy Lopez. We open e4, Black meets e5, and the knight develops to f3.
Black develops to c6 and we pin with the bishop to b5 — the Ruy Lopez.
Black plays d6 — the Steinitz Variation. It's fine, and doesn't change our approach; note that ...d6 sets up a pin of its own.
To exploit that pin we open the centre. The Ruy offers two roads — c3 preparing d4, or the immediate d4, which is perfectly good; after ...exd4 we recapture with the knight.
Black defends with the bishop to d7.
Now a hard-to-grasp move: we capture on c6. You'd think the whole point was to keep that bishop, but there's a deeper idea here.

We are pressing and keeping the pin — White stands better. There is a buffet of captures, and the e5-point is not going anywhere: Black will not take on d4 himself, as it disastrously opens the e-file, so we can round that pawn up in due course, with Black's queenside wrecked and our pieces active. But careful: a mindless bishop to e3 allows ...Rb8 hitting b2, and fianchettoing with b3 weakens the dark squares.
Black develops the knight to f6. Played right, this eventually forces Black to release the centre by taking on d4.
We castle. If Black grabs on e4, he opens the e-file — and once his bishop lands on e4 we get a big initiative.
We recapture on e4 with the knight.
Black recaptures with the bishop on e4. How do we hit it while improving?
The rook to e1 — we can reclaim the e5-pawn later, no hurry; the rook attacks down the file and adds a pin.
